study.title: Amos 6 False security, empty pleasure and unavoidable judgment
study.overview: Amos 6 denounces the self-confidence of leaders and people accommodated in Zion and Samaria, who treated the divine threat as if it were distant and irrelevant. The chapter shows that the problem is not only political or military, but spiritual: the elite lives in luxury, ignores the ruin of the people and trusts in human advantages, while God announces that this security will be broken. The text ends with a bitter irony: the border and the recovered territory will not be proof of permanent force, but the exact space of enemy oppression.

outline.title: Arrogant comfort and misleading comparison
outline.explanation: The first verses cast an "I"s" against those who live quietly in Zion and Samaria. The prophet confronts the sense of national superiority and the impression that the day of judgment is far off. The comparison with other kingdoms shows that Israel and Judah had no reason to boast of strength or privilege.

outline.title: Luxury, music and indifference to suffering
outline.explanation: Here Amos describes an excess lifestyle: ivory beds, fine food, music, wine and perfumes. Central sin is not only to enjoy, but to live this pleasure without grieve by the "ruin of Joseph, that is, without compassion for the disgrace of the people of God.

outline.title: The banquet ends and death enters the house
outline.explanation: The prophet announces that the accommodated will be the first to go into exile. The Lord, swearing for himself, declares hatred for Jacob's arrogance and palaces. The picture becomes gloomy: few will remain, and even the funerary rites will be marked by silence and calamity.

outline.title: The perversion of judgment and the invasion of the entire limit
outline.explanation: Amos uses images of absurdity in nature to show that Israel has made judgment in poison and justice in bitterness. The false joy for military conquests is denied: the same territorial range celebrated as victory will be the way in which an oppressive nation will advance against Israel.

study.context: The chapter assumes the division between Judah and Israel and speaks of Zion and Samaria as fortified centers, that is, the citadels associated with the two political realities. The notes inform that Calne, Hamate and Gath had already suffered judgment in previous times, which serves as a warning: Israel would be no exception. The announced end involves the action of Assyria, which, according to the notes, led Israel into captivity and marked the fulfillment of the threat.
study.theology: Amos 6 teaches that national security, material prosperity and religious tradition do not nullify the righteousness of God. The Lord opposes arrogance when it produces moral indifference, and condemns a worship or a public life that enjoys goods without caring about the ruin of others. The divine oath emphasizes the firmness of judgment: God not only advises, but decrees. Theologically, the chapter confronts the separation between faith and compassion, showing that the prosperity without fear of the Lord becomes evidence of spiritual blindness. There is also irony: what seemed to be territorial expansion and stability ends up being the scene of foreign oppression. In evangelical reading, the text calls God's people to examine whether their trust is in external advantages or in the Lord Himself, and whether their joy is accompanied by justice, repentance and mercy.

scholarViews.insight: Trust in physical power and strongholds is sin; the text shows that both Judah and Israel presumptuously rely on the citadels of Zion and Samaria instead of relying on God.
The section describes people who surrender to pleasure and treat God's threats as light, while divine sentence falls with severity over these sensualists.
The verse points to the punishment for the Assyrian sword, which would come upon Israel after its false security and its rejection of God.

questions: In what areas of life am I treating God's warning as if judgment were too far to affect me?
Have I enjoyed the goods I receive without realizing the spiritual, moral and social need of the people around me?
Is my practical trust in God or in economic stability, human structure, position and control?
study.practice: This chapter calls the discipline of repentance before the crisis imposes it. The concrete application is to review where our security is placed: comfort, heritage, status, tradition or power. It also asks for active compassion: it is not enough to avoid private sins; one must perceive the ruin that reaches others and respond with care, justice and solidarity. An objective practice would be to pray and act this week for someone in visible need, and at the same time to renounce a habit of consumption or ostentation that feeds spiritual indifference.
study.uncertainty: The given notes do not detail each poetic expression of the chapter, and some points are in probable interpretation, not in absolute statement. In particular, there are differences between commentators regarding certain historical and translation details, such as reading some terms on burial at 6:10 and the exact identification of ancient places in 6:2 and 6:14. There is also a confessional reading in Adam Clarke on musical instruments, but it should be understood as interpretative opinion, not as a consensus required by the text.
